claims.text: RFC 9457 defines the Problem Details JSON object (media type application/problem+json) with five optional members - type, title, status, detail, instance - plus API-defined extension members; it is a standard error format for HTTP APIs, not the only permitted one.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9457, section 3 ("The Problem Details JSON Object")

claims.text: RFC 9457: the type member is optional; when it is not present, its value is assumed to be "about:blank", meaning the problem has no more specific semantics than the HTTP status code alone.

RFC 9457: the status member is the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence; it is only advisory, and generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response, which stays authoritative.

The Caddyfile's @missingOrder handler responds to a missing order with status 404, header Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8, and body {"error":"order not found"} — one ad-hoc field, no standard shape.

The Caddyfile's /conflict handler responds with status 409 and the plain-text body "Conflict: this order was already paid", with no Content-Type header set in the handler (Caddy's respond directive defaults to text/plain for a plain string).

RFC 9457 section 1: Problem Details can be used with any HTTP status code, but most naturally fits 4xx and 5xx responses; it is not limited to 5xx server errors. Its worked examples use 403 and 422, both client errors.

Live this session: GET /conflict on the running lab (localhost:8080) returns HTTP 409, Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8, Content-Length: 37, and the exact body "Conflict: this order was already paid" — no JSON, no error field.
claims.source_hint: live curl this session: curl -sS -i http://localhost:8080/conflict

claims.text: RFC 9457: the type member is a JSON string containing a URI reference that identifies the problem type, not a plain sentence; absolute URIs are recommended when possible.
RFC 9457: title SHOULD NOT change from occurrence to occurrence of a problem type, except for localization; detail is specific to this occurrence and typically does vary.

RFC 9110: 400 means the server considers the request malformed or otherwise invalid; 404 means the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource (or is unwilling to disclose that one exists); 409 means the request conflicts with the current state of the target resource.
